name: No Rest for the Wicked
review:
Tentative recommend.
Fun gameplay, unique fusions of different genres, and beautiful game world and graphics.

Issues/things to be aware of:
Weird periodic performance drops and issues, possibly due to optimization. Kinda grindy in some ways, but not in a fun or normal grindy way, more like a "this upgrade requires you to get tons of resources and should scale based on how many players are in the guild/world" kind of grindy. Think like how Warframe does guild grinding and how it scales to the size of the guild, this game needs that functionality for the town upgrade costs.
Some armor is just stupidly heavy for zero reason and it's difficult to reasonably wear. (nitpick)
Movement controls are janky, but tolerable for me as a veteran of both diablo-like arpgs and soulslikes, but many will find it frustrating and too clunky.
The roguelite dungeon mode is too long for what it offers, especially as a distraction from the main mode. The boss is also just outright unfair if you go in underleveled. Should really just scale to level when you first find it or have a periodic level increase since there's different difficulties anyways. Lock the related quest to finding it behind a level minimum so people don't waste time trying it on a character that's never going to be able to handle it adequately.

name: Sun Haven
review:
This game is good if you're a casual player. It has a mode to make the game quite cosy. Invincibility during fighting, getting rid of pets on your farm, adding sparkles on ready crops, and you can tailor the length of your day to be a fast 15 minutes or a leisurely 40 min irl, stuff like that. The storyline is non-intrusive but interesting, the lands are very imaginative, the skill lines and skill points make you feel like you're nearly constantly progressing and getting better, and the different types of crops are creative and interesting. I also find the fishing, a simple timed game of no more than two taps (one to hook the fish and initiate the mini game and one to actually catch the fish), one of the few fishing mechanics that is very accessible to those with limited mobility. It presents a very light challenge, with power ups to make it easier as you skill up. There's distinct world areas, with their own farming locations to enjoy, there's reasonably interesting characters, and there's magic and different character races for those that enjoy a bit of whimsy with their farming sim.

That being said, the game is quite grindy as well. You need a lot of materials nearly all the time, especially if you'd like to unlock areas in the mine for daily use or finish the museum. Most are familiar with museum mechanics, so that's not too surprising, but this game is not balanced as far as its RNG. Get used to seeing every single item but the one you actually need VERY often. There is no accomadation to drop the items you need more often vs those you clearly have. If you're a 100%-er, you will likely find it frustrating to know you must push through that issue AND marry every character in town, which is nothing more than a time-waster.

All in all it's a good casual game for those that like Harvest Moon, Stardew Valley, and others of the genre. It has its flaws, but is a good addition to your farming-sim game sessions. (also Snackos suck, just fyi)
note: grindy game

name: STAR WARS Zero Company™
review:
I was a huge fan of modern XCOM 1 + 2 and Midnight Suns, so Zero Company was one of the games I've been the most hyped for in the last few years. You can't really come up with a better setting than Star Wars for former Firaxis XCOM Devs to cook inside of. I was also just glad to see the tactics genre get another big release.

Unfortunately, I have never before felt so uninterested in finishing a tactics game. I'm around cycle 21, and the game's maximum length before forcing you to finish the campaign is cycle 40. I looked up all of the remaining content to see if I was missing out on anything that would change my mind but it really only further reinforced my opinion of the game. It feels like they forgot so much of what made XCOM and Midnight Suns fun. My negative review has nothing to do with any bugs, as I didn't really experience any outside of a few wonky overwatches that still ultimately worked.

This is one of the most repetitive games I've ever played:
-Every mission I play feels nearly identical after the first few. It's always some minor objective, and constant enemy respawns. Enemy variety is the weakest it's ever been. The environments are HEAVILY simplified compared to XCOM, where you went in and out of buildings that gave you different approaches with cover and the ability to use explosives to shape the area in your favor. This exists at a very very bare minimum level in this game and there are no buildings to take cover inside of.
-Your characters start out with every ability their class will ever have, and all your skill ups do is increase the potency of the abilities. It's pretty damn hard to come up with another tactics game that has progression where your character never learns a new skill for their class. Yes, you do get dual-classing later, but you're just picking two classes that you already had individual access to, and putting both on one character.
-All of the upgrades in this game are very uninspired. Whether it's weapon mods, focus points, bond levels, or facility upgrades, everything is just tiny extra stat bonuses that feel just barely impactful and don't do much at all to change how you approach the game
-The game doesn't really give you enough credits, so you always just feel like you're scraping by, meaning you don't really have enough currency to even attempt to make that many changes between battles.
-Skill rotations end up being the same all the time. What percentage of players do you think beat this game using Combat Recon -> Web Darts -> Web Surge -> Repeat. Probably a lot.

Playing this game just feels like being stuck in the mud. It feels like very little is changing between fights.

Some other complaints:
-The Anakin Skywalker levels were the first time in a tactics game that I felt like a series of battles were handed to the player pretty much already "solved". His first 2 levels basically play themselves and it's really really obvious that you use his one shotting light saber throw to kill all the enemies lined up or his 1 shotting melee once per round and the levels are over. They might as well be cutscenes.
-One of the biggest selling points of XCOM 2 was the ability to customize your squad. This was also one of the biggest selling points of Zero Company. But then they made the strongest characters in the game all unique story characters that you could not customize the appearances of. I thought it'd be really obvious that customizable Jedi and Bounty Hunters would be nice, but all you get are Tel-Rea and Cly, who both have unique abilities that no other characters can get.
-I'm not a fan of how they're leaning into the miniature open-world component that Midnight Suns introduced. It doesn't really add anything meaningful to the gameplay whatsoever. It's just a glorified cutscene that the player has to move himself through instead of letting the cutscene play itself.
-Why did we force the story missions to tick down so quickly? XCOM and Midnight suns allowed for the player to take longer if they wanted to experiment more, and this feels like a step backwards. Who knows, maybe it's because they realized their game had no variety, and they wanted to push people out before it became even more obvious.
-The removal of fog of war, hurt the game, especially when combined when the lack of enemy variety. XCOM's opening phase felt very tense, because you had to take space methodically and carefully and try not to overstep, utilizing overwatch and cover to progress. The enemy variety in XCOM also made you unsure if you'd suddenly walk into some strong alien you've never encountered before. There's very little tension in this game, if any at all.
-XCOM 2 had 6 player squads. Zero Company has...4 player squads????


Upsides:
Story was fairly decent. Heavy amounts of optional exposition wasn't for me but I can't complain that it's in the game for those that want it.
There is a good enough foundation that a solid expansion like XCOM 2: WOTC could actually make this game legitimately good if they just gave it more content variety and revamp the progression system to actually feel good.

For now, I recommend anyone that enjoyed this game to try out XCOM 2. It came out almost 11 years ago and feels light years ahead.
note: boring, repetitive missions, lost what made previous games fun

name: Dressmaker
review:
Good games deserve good reviews! ❤️

A hidden gem among simulators!

We have so many shop simulators on Steam, and honestly, I think we're all getting a little tired of them. But this game feels like a breath of fresh air!

I really fell in love with this game!

Of course, it has a few bugs, but the developers are trying to fix them as quickly as they can.

On the other hand, you have to cut, sew and combine so many different pieces. It takes quite a bit of time and can feel a little tedious, but it also makes the whole experience feel so realistic!

When the game was first released, I had some problems with the patterns while making my first dresses. I couldn't understand exactly what I was supposed to cut.

And guess what? Just THREE DAYS later, the developers released an update with pattern previews!

GENIUS!

Another thing I absolutely love is the characters. Each of them has their own personality, and they don't all look or feel the same. It's such a refreshing detail that makes the game feel even more special.

Overall, this game feels like something genuinely new in a genre that's become a little repetitive. ❤️

name: Approximately Up
review:
The concept behind this game is fantastic, and I genuinely want to love it. The engineering systems, aerodynamics, electronics, and spacecraft construction have enormous potential.

Unfortunately, the sheer amount of manual work makes the experience more tedious than enjoyable. Having to physically route every power and signal cable, even when building relatively simple control circuits, becomes exhausting. On top of that, there's no apparent way to use my physical joystick to control the in-game joysticks.

I'm not asking for simpler engineering or physics. I'm asking for better tools to interact with them.

Honestly, if this game had automatic cable routing or native joystick support—even just one of those features—I could easily see myself spending a thousand hours playing it.

I really hope the developers consider these improvements, because there's an incredible game underneath all that friction.
note: manual work becomes tedious

name: Dead by Daylight
review:
NOT RECOMMENDED - The game is currently in an unplayable and unfair state 

The developers have completely ruined the game balance with an undeniable bias toward Killers (with the average Kill rate sitting at a staggering 60%). The Survivor experience has been completely gutted, not just for Solo Queue, but for full coordinated teams (SWF) as well. 

Major issues currently destroying the game:

Movement & Visual Glitches: Due to broken haste stacking and Bloodlust mechanics, Killers visually lag and "skate/slide" across the ground, making looping and distance calculation impossible.
Broken Hitboxes & Pallet Delay: Outdated capsule hitboxes register unfair hits through solid walls. Furthermore, a highly disruptive Pallet Drop Delay has surfaced, causing actions to lag and giving Killers unearned downs.
Oppressive Meta Against Teams: Massive adjustments encourage toxic playstyles like heavy Tunneling, hard Slugging, and Face-camping, combined with unaddressed generator regression combos (Scourge Hook: Pain Resonance + Hex: Ruin) that easily crush full teams.
Catastrophic Server Failures & Unjust Penalties: Dedicated servers are constantly failing, resulting in sudden 200ms ping spikes. Even worse, server crashes constantly trigger random player disconnections (DCs) mid-match—even when our own internet connection is completely stable and flawless. This ruins the match for the entire team, while the game’s flawed system unjustly punishes the victims with matchmaking penalties.
Profit Over Player Satisfaction: It is highly evident that Behaviour Interactive prioritizes monetization through the non-stop release of paid cosmetics and new licensed killers, while completely neglecting core game fixes. The developers treat the game more like a storefront than an asymmetrical multiplayer experience that requires stable servers and fair balancing, proving that profit comes before community feedback.

Behaviour Interactive refuses to listen to community feedback. Save your time and money.
note: roles are unbalanced, strong meta, glitches, profit focus over community

The game looks very pretty. But that's about it. It was either not play-tested at all, or what I find more worrying, intentionally designed to waste as much time as possible while making the player feel mizerable. Every mechanic, every interaction produces friction:
2 buildings touch corners? can't pass there
'active bag': no your inventory is not full, you need to go there and click the bag with an empty slot
factory building: go across the whole area to open the plan view. no you can't place that because your 9x9 inventory doesnt have the right part out of 20 needed for building. go home, get it, place a workstation. run to the workstation to 'build' it. run back to place conveyors. made a mistake? enter 'delete' mode. run back to pick up parts because now they block the build area. run back to build point. repeat ad nauseum
pin a recipe? lmao
recipe list? nope
tooltips? sometimes, and not where you need them
tutorials? google.com

It just feels very underbaked. Like they had an idea, somehow hired incredible pixel artists and either rushed or vibecoded the rest.

name: Valheim
review:
Game design decisions questionable. 

You have these raids that basically zerg you with no real answer early game. You don't have weapons that do quick enough cleave or aoe a large mob. 

Mechanically, you do have parry, for 1 target at a time. In a zerg, you can only parry a few, with no real progress. There's no way of actually hitting back since you are continuously parrying. 

The events last for, I believe 2 minutes, so you are just basically running around in circle for no reason, other than to just end the event. If you enjoy running around in circle in these events, then sure this is the game for you.

I can't think of another reason that these mechanics exist, other than to increase the play hours on a game with poor design decisions.

I am assuming mid or late game, there would be more answers? Even then, combats really not that enjoyable. Parry is pretty straight forward and simple. Not a whole lot of patterns you'd truly have to deal with.

You spend alot of time running around either back to your body, because you got zerged. 

Or suddenly dying because an event happens RIGHT when you sleep away the night. And you can't do anything because now you are stuck in the sleep process. You have no way of responding to the event.

Boat travelling is incredibly slow, even if you luckily get the wind behind your sails. So if you die somewhere else, better pray that you crafted a portal on the same island.

I spent more time running/sailing to things that are not objective related.
note: frustrating combat

name: ACE COMBAT 8: WINGS OF THEVE
review:
After 7 years, the newest entry to Ace Combat is here! And this is quite possibly the best to date.

Project Aces took their time and it has paid off; every system and part of the game is more polished than before. Without going into any spoilers, the campaign is a long but satisfying journey through a war torn Usea (but when isn't Usea at war?). And the narrative makes more sense than ever, but don't worry! There's still plenty of whacky strangereal shenanigans. A vibrant supporting cast brings the story to life and they get enough screen time and development for me to care about them.

Flying feels different and, in my opinion, better. Planes have weight to them so there's a slight delay to turning and there's also some momentum when you stop. But that feeling of heft makes the planes feel heavier and more realistic. Improvements to the camera allow better views of the action of the battlefield. There's lots of new little things that make the gameplay a good balance between familiar and fresh, and there's settings that let you tune that further.

The combat is simply great! Big battlefields filled with friend and foe. The mission variety keeps everything interesting, and there's plenty inspired by missions from previous games. Ground attack aircraft finally get their time to shine as there's plenty of stages for them to unleash their payloads of 4AGM or UGB with prejudice!

And the music is as amazing as ever! Dynamic music matching the gameplay is something games have been doing for a while now, but it hits different at 40,000 feet. I haven't heard a piece of music in this game I didn't like, but there's a few that are stuck in my head on repeat. My mind is just waiting for the soundtrack to drop.

Overall, I highly recommend Ace Combat 8 as a solid game for fans of Ace Combat and newcomers alike. It is IMO Project Ace's best work so far and I look forward to seeing you in the skies.

name: Cloudpunk
review:
After playing for 2.5 hours, I kinda wished the "intro" would end.

Fly to nav point. Park at the parking spot for the neighborhood, move on foot, talk to people, go back. It's all very linear and closed, with the megacity as the backdrop. You do get to make decisions. Like "go to this alternate nav point" to be more or less selfish / reliable. Or you could try to talk to random people and make them act like they are the ones talking to us.

At some point, you do get to visit "home" for a bit and there you can buy upgrades, so I assumed there would be some day cycle… but no, back to work! The whole games takes about 8 hours and is your first shift for cloudpunk in the city.

The voice actors do great work, they make the story. Without them, I don't think I would have paid too much attention to the story - and that leaves the game with not much else.

There is the core theme of CORA and the city having some kind of breakdowns, but you yourself don't witness much of that. Then there are automata and androids - but like with many of the other ideas explored, we only get a few singular moments that don't form a cohesive whole. It's a mix of tropes and short stories that take place in the same city to be "cyberpunk". There are food stalls in the rainy neon glow city to be cyberpunk. There are CEOs ordering pizza, scientists testing viruses, androids running a company for hundreds of years and AIs destined to be vacuum cleaners - sometimes silly, sometimes serious - because that's the kind of thing people would expect to find in a cyberpunk game.

The Voxel look is alright. It would have made more sense to me, if there was more destruction going on. Without textures, the buildings look cleaner and more sterile than they could have. The clouds above the city look eerie and beautiful - good job on those. A big problem is the map view: Because the neon-3d isn't the easiest to navigate, you have a minimap in the lower right. Now, what do you look at? The Traffic? No, your eyes will regularly return to the minimap. The city only exists for the backdrop of the story, and I barely looked at it. I couldn't tell you what connects to where. Follow the nav point in the lower right!

If you are an absolute fan of everything cyberpunk, you probably own the game and are happy with it. If you are looking for great gameplay, you won't find it here. I don't mind a story focused game, but this feels very bare bones in most regards.
note: repetitive gameplay, graphics could be better, intro took too long

name: Palworld
review:
The game itself is very well-made and enjoyable, but I am extremely dissatisfied with how the official servers are handled.

On official servers, if you don't log in for just 3 days (72 hours), your base and all your Pals are completely deleted. There is literally no way to recover them, meaning all the time and effort you invested goes completely to waste.

I understand this might be a countermeasure against server load, but the grace period is way too short. It creates a highly stressful situation where you feel forced to log in just to keep your progress from being wiped out, rather than logging in to actually enjoy the game.

Furthermore, this system creates a terrible double-whammy: players whose data gets wiped lose all motivation to return, which in turn leads to dead, unpopulated servers.

Multiplayer is fun, but official servers are only enjoyable in the very beginning. In the end, all my Pals, crafted equipment, and items were wiped. This is the ultimate fate that awaits you if you choose to play on official servers.
note: complaint on server limitations

review:
Can't remember how I found this game, doesn't matter. First game I've ever bought the dlc just to give the devs extra money.

Music- 11/10 (... Seriously. It's that good)

Replayability-10/10

UI - 6/10 but easy enough with some practice

Game play - 8/10. One shot deaths are frustrating, but you can one shot the bad guys as well.

Story- 5/10. Not great but in all fairness they are adding more story lines, this is early access right now. I think the true gem is that every game should and will be different, which makes it's own story each time.

Graphics- 4/10 but who gives a ****, that's part of the reason I bought it. I can run this on my Wi-Fi dishwasher

Difficulty- **** me / 10. Ok this is probably the worst gripe I and many others have. Difficulty has a steep ramp up if you're not paying attention. Mission Difficulty is not explained properly, HOWEVER, there are great guides that have allowed me to remedy this lapse so not game breaking. Read some guides, join discord group, and this issue literally reverses exponentially with player skill level.

Ultimately, this game is bad to the bone, it's difficult, the devs and community are great and it's worth full price.

If you like Rimworld, XCOM, Darkest Dungeon, FTL, Void War, or any other perma-decision/perma-death type games, then I think you will love this.

name: Heroes of Might and Magic: Olden Era
review:
UI and UX needs some work, but its not the worst problem with the current shape of the game.

You buy the "new Heroes", wanting to immerse yourself in this fantasy realm of might and magic, and the immersion falls flat very quickly. And its not due to UX issues.

After doing the tutorial you jump into the campaign just to realise how uninspired it is. Both in design and story. You pick "intended difficulty" and very soon find yourself steamrolling and asking yourself "why would i even bother gathering these resources, picking fights and capture buildings?" once you realise most of it gets reset every mission, and you hit the level cap for particular mission very quickly and you just need to move trough the necessary movement points to proceed with the story. The campaign so far seems like a chore to do, on a way to some fun that hopefully might be there somewhere (or not), instead of a great introduction and fun. The story isnt a redeeming quality here. Its silly and lackluster. Like done in a hurry to check the "story" box. There is no drama or anything creating feelings other then - what today's youth would call - a cringe humour.

I cant tell if the writers were tasked to make it silly on purpose or if its pretended seriousness humour. I dont know. It doesnt make me laugh, nor immerse me into it. There are no inspired concepts about anything. Just a copy paste cliches and crude, simple actors.

So at this point im questioning myself, whats the strong aspect of this game? I cant find any other than HOMM basic game's systems' design and the fact that its Heroes being developed. But without something built around it, with immersion and story it feels painfully dull.
note: poor story, boring gameplay, UI UX needs work

name: MIO: Memories in Orbit
review:
If you have obtained more than 4 golden strawberries from Celeste, or beat Hollow Knight, then go for it.

Is this game actually controller-compatible: NO, the movement design is keyboard-only.

This is a decent game, but not for chill, but more like the old arcade games that are relentless on tormenting or making sure you are frustrated, muting on paths they actually need a movement unlock to cross. You are expected to sweat and smash your desk hard due to dev-vibe and inconsistent designs.

The hardest part of this game involves movement, most bosses turns the floor to lava, mid-to-late game jump puzzles are crazy hard, and the map does not write any place names or mark your destination.

The graphics is lacking optimization, and somewhat dirty (especially the dirty halo around the player character and NPCs), playing on all graphic setting other than high looks like a mess, but still ok since it doesn't obstruct the player for seeing.

The audio & control has a dirty exit bug when exiting from map too early, some buttons just stop working, the player must exit to main menu and re-enter to fix it, which breaks immersion.

The reason I would recommend this game is mostly for having the basic movements consistent enough and manageable (keyboard only). However, all platforming sections are cursed due to mid-air attack issues:

Mid-air attack ranges are inconsistent due to camera angle shift, unfortunately the developer have tuned this movement for combat and sceneries
Mid-air attack up/down/forward is fundamentally crappy to joystick playthrough, this problem became a nightmare when hairpin hook movement is involved
Mid-air down-attack jump on NPCs does not restore stamina, yet it does on bombs, this inconsistent nonsense is never told just like most movement, until it became mandatory when player begins to enter the crucible

In contrast, Celest has secret movements too, but it DID show all the movements the player need to clear the level
101: You cannot expect the player to figure out everything magically
101: You cannot require the player to act in a secret way, and punish them for not doing so



Update: Changing to negative review since the boss fight with Sol & Vin was just too crappy and idiotic that ruins anything left good about this game. Tossing game design basics away to promote developer vibe is crossing the line. For example, only part of the issues in this one fight:

The player gets killed in only 2 hits no matter what
2/3 of the time were spent on traveling to boss room
Most boss attacks are full screen, because of the small area the player can stand on
Boss attack indicator is incredibly small, not only smaller than all enemy NPCs, but also covered by player's attack registering effect
Boss attack's reaction time is much shorter than human reflex
Boss HP is way too high for the speed and damage they have
The correct movement to beat this fight is inconsistent since the boss randomly teleports way too high up, out of clipping/hooking distance
Dodge becomes useless since the bosses are double and triple attacking quickly
String crawl becomes useless since there is no wall to climb on
Pay attention at the boss became useless since the floor turns to lava

review:
Winter Burrow is a charming survival adventure that takes the familiar pressures of gathering, crafting, and environmental danger and places them inside a much gentler, more personal experience. Developed by Pine Creek Games and published by Noodlecake, the game follows a small mouse returning from the big city to a childhood burrow, only to discover that the once-comfortable home has deteriorated and the aunt who was supposed to care for it has disappeared. This simple premise gives the survival mechanics an emotional purpose, since rebuilding the burrow is as much about reclaiming a home as it is about staying alive.

The frozen woodland serves as both a beautiful setting and the primary obstacle. Leaving the safety of the burrow means facing the elements while searching for resources needed for crafting, cooking, and restoration. Insect wildlife adds danger to exploration, preventing the surrounding wilderness from becoming completely harmless. However, the game deliberately avoids the relentless pressure associated with harsher survival titles. Players are encouraged to proceed at their own pace, making exploration feel more like a carefully prepared expedition than a desperate struggle against unforgiving systems.

Crafting is closely connected to everyday life. Materials gathered outside can be turned into useful tools and other necessities, but Winter Burrow also embraces activities that reinforce its cozy identity. Knitting warm sweaters and baking pies are practical extensions of survival rather than disconnected minigames. Preparing for another journey becomes part of a comfortable routine in which gathering, crafting, cooking, and returning home naturally feed into one another.

Restoring the childhood burrow is one of the most satisfying elements because it provides a visible representation of progress. Instead of simply watching numbers increase or replacing equipment with stronger versions, players gradually transform a damaged home into an inviting living space. Decorating the interior provides additional personalization, while the prospect of eventually relaxing beside the fireplace gives all those trips into the wilderness a meaningful destination. The contrast between the cold outdoors and increasingly welcoming interior is central to the game's atmosphere.

The experience also understands that surviving alone would undermine its warmer themes. Other woodland inhabitants can be encountered during the adventure, giving players opportunities to make friends and expand their survival handbook. These relationships help make the world feel inhabited rather than functioning purely as a resource map. At the same time, the disappearance of the protagonist's aunt provides an ongoing mystery. Searching for answers gives exploration a narrative motivation beyond simply finding another supply of crafting materials.

Character customization and player choice further support the relaxed philosophy. Rather than demanding one optimized route through its systems, the game allows players to shape their mouse, decorate their home, and pursue a path that better suits their preferred approach. This flexibility is especially appropriate for a cozy survival game because it reduces the sense that every minute needs to be spent maximizing efficiency. There is still progression and danger, but the experience leaves room for simply enjoying the environment and developing the burrow.

The hand-drawn visual direction is particularly well suited to the concept. Snow-covered woodland environments, tiny household objects, knitted clothing, food, insects, and the mouse protagonist create something resembling an interactive illustrated storybook. The art helps establish warmth without eliminating the vulnerability of being a tiny creature in a large wilderness. That contrast gives the setting personality and makes returning to the safety of the burrow after an expedition especially satisfying.

Its relaxed structure may not appeal equally to everyone. Players who prefer brutal survival mechanics, complicated combat, or constant threats may find its deliberate pacing too forgiving. Resource gathering can also become repetitive in games built around crafting loops, particularly when familiar areas must be revisited. Much of the enjoyment consequently depends on whether the player appreciates slower activities such as gathering supplies, decorating, cooking, knitting, exploring, and gradually improving a home.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable rather than Verified. The game works with the default controller configuration, displays appropriate controller icons, and its default graphics configuration performs appropriately on the handheld. The main compatibility concern is that some in-game text can be small and potentially difficult to read on the Steam Deck's display. This prevents it from receiving the highest compatibility classification, but otherwise its controller-oriented gameplay and relatively relaxed structure make it naturally suitable for portable sessions.

Winter Burrow ultimately stands out because its individual mechanics revolve around a consistent idea of rebuilding a home. Gathering wood or other materials is connected to restoration, warm clothing has practical importance in the winter environment, friendships contribute to surviving and understanding the woodland, and exploration gradually reveals what happened to the missing aunt. Even ordinary survival activities therefore contribute to the broader narrative rather than existing solely because the genre traditionally requires them.

The result is a thoughtful combination of cozy life simulation, exploration, crafting, resource management, and accessible survival mechanics. It does not attempt to make survival relentlessly stressful, instead finding satisfaction in preparation, discovery, companionship, and watching a ruined childhood home slowly become comfortable again. Players looking for extreme difficulty may want something harsher, but those attracted to atmospheric exploration and gradual progression should find plenty to appreciate.

Winter Burrow offers a warm and distinctive interpretation of survival gameplay, strengthened by its beautiful hand-drawn presentation, meaningful home restoration, enjoyable crafting activities, gentle progression, and underlying family mystery. Its Steam Deck Playable status also makes it a good handheld option, provided the smaller interface text is not an issue.

Rating: 9/10

name: Shroom and Gloom
review:
This is a fun take on the deck builder. The general gameplay has a higher focus on healing during play and gives you lots of cards to support that, in contrast to other deck builders. I've played a few and this one feels pretty fresh, with some fun new card ideas and interactions. 

I like the idea that your cards scale as you play them and use them effectively. The "On fatal" effect can either improve the cards or give you some sort of secondary benefit, like energy or food to heal. This ads a pretty interesting dimension to how you play your cards.

I also like the parallel camping game. You switch back and forth between fighting monsters and setting up camp, which has a different set of cards. I like that the camp it not just a stop to heal, it's also another way to upgrade your cards and skills, heal, and get new cards. There isn't the typical "choose 1 of 3" at the end of each battle.

The faux-3D movement is pretty cool looking, like walking through a cardboard diorama. Overall the line drawing style takes a bit off the edge off the, frankly, gross cards. I'd hate for a more realistic rendering of goop or guts or whatever.

It is still early days, so the controller support is not great, but it works mostly well enough, which is important for my RSI.

I've only seen a few bugs, at least one of which was already fixed. No crashes, and saving works well. This is a solid early access game.

Online racing is working well enough, I had some fun races and you can clearly see what they are aiming to do.

Optimization is a thing in this game. It works on my setup (Ryzen 5 7600x3d and Radeon 7900XTX) pretty well, but especially in online races I had some crashes. Lowering the graphics settings helped, but they still have a job to do there.

Talking about graphics: This game is beautiful, an improvement from ACC, which already was really good looking.

The reason for the negative reviews is that Kunos decided to scrab the career mode. This is annoying, I was looking foreward to the open world and an in depth career experience coming with it.

But still the driving is just so fun that I still look positively on this game. It is fundermentally really good and I am very hopeful that this might be my next main sim.

name: Lost Ark
review:
10% of this game: The most brilliant and dopamine fueled class, combat, and boss design I've ever experienced in any video game ever.
90% of this game: Degrading busywork, abusive RNG progression, absurd menu bloat, and overpriced microtransactions.

The above facts are mentally and emotionally inescapable. I thought about it every time I wasted hours getting trapped in a raid through no fault of my own on a weekly basis; every time I threw away weeks worth of gold and materials on failed progression attempts; every time my interest in a new class release was repressed by the realization that I didn't even have time to play the existing ones; every time my hope and excitement for a new boss was crushed by the math showing that the rewards would not offset the progression and opportunity cost of accessing that boss until after 6-12 months of repeating it weekly.

Equalized content used to be the way to enjoy the 10% without subjecting yourself to the 90%, but the developers have removed it with no announced plans to replace it, and all of their recent efforts indicate that they never will. After quitting cold turkey over a year ago, I decided to give it another try with the recent anniversary event, and I could not put up with it for more than one day. For the first time in years I saw the game through the lens of a new player and it's truly repulsive. Even with my years of knowledge, experience, progress, achievements, and accumulated wealth worth literally thousands of dollars, I couldn't bring myself to chase the now rotten carrot on the stick. Best of luck to any new players starting with nothing.
note: busywork, menu bloat, microsactions

name: Sea of Stars: Sunset Edition
review:
This is a really hard game to say I don't recommend because in theory I should love everything about it. The setting, the combat, the level design, the music, the sprite work oh my god - but despite getting to the late game, I never finished it, and I don't really feel any desire to whatsoever despite all the things about it that hypothetically I should have loved.

In spite of a thousand little things that should work in its favor, the game is ultimately just kind of boring. The characters are boring and very flat overall with little in the way of memorability, and the story does do some interesting things but it all just feels... flat. Despite so much of the game being incredible in a void, there's so little personality to so much of it that it feels like a waste of time. Playing Sea of Stars is a very strange experience because I was beyond engrossed at the start when the story was kind of just a generic fantasy tale, but as the game went on and the story got more interesting, I somehow managed to get more and more bored of the whole thing because the characters themselves are so tepid that nothing feels as though it has the impact it should and the only character I remotely cared about ends up intentionally distancing themselves from anything of real consequence.

Then there's the combat, which at first feels like an excellent blend of Mario & Luigi and Chrono Trigger with a cool and unique mechanic that revolves around hitting enemies with a specifc amount of specific elemental attacks to "break" them and stop their attack in its tracks. Again, theoretically awesome, but by even the mid-game it wears out its welcome and instead becomes obnoxious as it requires combinations that are genuinely impossible to pull off before they attack, so you end up just eating damage regardless, even if dealing some of this elemental damage does lower the damage you take.

This is compounded and made infinitely worse by two things: The fact that there's no such thing as a "flee" button in this game while enemies simultaneously have complex mechanics and a lot of health eventually makes combat a completely tedious slog - and the fact that any meaningful new combat abilities are very few and far between, makes level progress feel like garbage and combat feel extremely samey.

I honestly could've forgiven all of this, but the secret here is that before I was about to complete the game, I learned that you don't actually get to fight the villain and truly conclude the story until you also complete every single sidequest in the game, and collect a metric ton of hidden items that have no real indication you should be doing so, as they only give you relatively middling rewards from a single NPC with no plot relevance. This is, roughly speaking, like if Paper Mario didn't let you fight Bowser and blueballed you with no conclusion until you collected every single Star Piece in the game. Awful. This, along with the creeping boredom I was experiencing, immediately killed any and all desire I had to finish the game.

I'm actually really sad writing this review because I do think these developers have so much potential and their other game ( The Messenger ) is fantastic - but I just can't bring myself to say I actually liked this. I hate that I feel this way, and I hate that I'm saying this, but I would honestly skip this one. Despite incredible sprite art, music, and atmosphere at times, it's a truly charmless experience.
note: boring game, flat story, combat wears out

name: Bodycam
review:
The matchmaking system is very poor, if you do regular quickplay you are often in servers with 50% of the players being bots as well as experiencing issues with staying connected. You are forced to use the Lobby Browser, which is manageable but annoying. Even still, if the person who created the lobby disconnects the entire server will shut down on the spot. 

The progression basically doesn't exist. There is a currency you can spend to unlock new guns and attachments, but you unlock everything important very very quickly. The way you earn the currency is lacking as well, it's a base amount for winning a match, plus a certain amount per kill. For some reason, you also earn a percentage less of it depending on which match type you play. TDM, Gun Game. and others earn you less than Hardpoint. While there are a lot of things you can purchase in the loadout editor, there is no real reason to purchase the vast majority of them. A lot of them are purely cosmetic, many of the attachments are versions of another with miniscule differences. You cannot change your knife or grenade at all, and you can't change anything non-cosmetic about your drone. After 5 hours, you essentially have access to everything of substance.

The only ranked mode is a 2v2 plant and defuse style game, which I found frustrating as I didn't enjoy it very much. Otherwise, ranked gameplay is simply +/- Elo at the end of every match. No titles for ranks and no rewards or other structure at all. 

The gameplay is genuinely incredibly fun, but this is basically a skeleton of a game concept and lacks anything that would draw me back into the game. 

Don't be like me and spend $30 expecting a semi-polished game

name: Digimon Story Time Stranger
review:
If I could, I would give this game a NEUTRAL RATING. Overall, it's a great game, but the sidekicks have ruined the whole experience for me. So here's the thing: In the demo, it feels like you are the hero of the story, and only at the end of it, you get to know Inori (sidekick no. 1). She is incredibly whiny and annoying, repeats obvious facts, and all you can do is agree with her. This was still fine. However, later on, Aegimon joins your group (sidekick no. 2), and he basically doubles the Inori experience. I was like, okay, let's just skip their cutscenes and focus on the actually good gameplay. But it gets worse. Basically, later in the story, the characters stop seeing you as the hero/protagonist and give Aegimon all the credit for your work, turning him into the hero/protagonist of the story so much that in many conversations, you don't even get addressed by the other characters anymore.

If I had been aware of this before purchasing the game, I would not have bought it.

If I had to compare the sidekick feel, I would say it's close to companions from Pokémon Sun/Moon and Pokémon Sword/Shield, but instead of them being overly cheerful, they are overly whiny. On top of that, the lady on the phone (forgot her name) basically only tells you: Ah, yes, what you're experiencing fits our notes, continue, also your dead father is dead, and he would have loved this. That doesn't make me care, and it's honestly just annoying after the tenth time.

I kind of feel lied to by the demo,

The sidekicks make me feel like I'm not the hero of this story and like my actions don't matter. I have been taking larger and larger breaks from the game, and I don't know if I will have the motivation to finish it. At some point, I realized that it's because of these two characters. I wish there were some way to remove them, through a mod or something.

If the next game has annoying sidekicks like this again, I will not buy it.

POSITIVES:
However, I want to be very clear: Besides that, this is a great game! If you don't care about the issues I addressed, you should absolutely go for it. The combat is great, the world feels alive, I love the graphics on both pc and Steam Deck, the music is fun, grinding for Digimon feels incredibly satisfying, it has this fun mini card game I really enjoy, and the story and background characters (excluding the sidekicks) are enjoyable as well.

If you are on the fence about getting this game, this is what I would recommend:
- Watch a Let's Play part that includes Inori and Aegimon to see if they bother you or not
- Play the demo to see if you find the base game mechanics satisfying
- Get the game on sale without DLC, so you don't regret spending too much money if you end up disliking it

I was very unsure whether I should mark this as recommended or not. I decided to go with don't recommend so it's easier for others to find criticism. I also checked the box to allow comments so other players can share their thoughts about the sidekicks below my review.
note: annoying companions

name: Approximately Up
review:
Can't stay below Overwhelmingly Positive for long, I'll make sure of it! So long as you know this game is trying to be complicated, and actually requires you to think things through from an engineering perspective, it's very very good at what it does. There are plenty of accessibility features that were completely left out (likely on purpose) that make things less approachable from a wider gaming perspective -- such as ZERO timewarp, the fact that everything must be placed by hand, and no navigational aids such as maps of the solar system -- but it follows the rules it lays out 100% of the time, and every challenge in the game feels amazing to work out because it never tries to hold your hand through it. And Co-op is downright incredible if the person you're playing with is as committed to the building of ships as you are, and you both work together to keep it running.

I repeat, this game isn't accessible in the ways other games are. Over two hours of my day were spent in space just waiting for my ship to accelerate and deccelerate, and it's FASCINATING. The scale of the world is never downplayed through making your trip pass at 1000x speed. Planets feel far and unreachable, and when you reach them, they have some of the prettiest scenery as a reward. It's for a very specific subset of people, but I think games should be judged on how well they achieve their goals, and with that logic this game is incredibly well done. :D

name: Still Wakes the Deep
review:
I think the best way to write a review is to break my thoughts into a few different parts. But, the TLDR; is that this game is a strong 8/10 and deserves a buy if you enjoy visual story experiences.

For the first part--I wouldn't say this is inherently a horror game. Although there are horror elements-really just body horror-there isn't really anything 'scary' to the game. The scariest part 
is messing up an item throw and not being able to find another to toss to distract the monster. This isn't a major issue though, as you can usually just run and get away. I think what does exist though is the perfect balance of cinematic horror elements that create an environment that is 'scary' but only due to a tense atmosphere. With the art style for the main monster thing there is a pretty remarkable sense of awe that the game gives you. This leads into point number two.

Point two is that the game plays like a movie. You could be watching the main character on screen play the game himself and from start to finish it would be entertaining. The game is beautiful. Max ultra graphics on a 2-4k screen really shows how much attention to detail the developers put into the game. It is gorgeous through and through, and the use of real photos / textures that were implemented strongly add to this. You can truly get lost into the game and start to question if you are watching real video. The one graphical thing that was a large let down though were the monsters that 'chase' you. They don't look good. They have strange and buggy AI. They glitch around and after the first encounter you have already seen the worst of it for the rest of the game. If they get up close, it almost looks like the texture is missing with how low poly and wonky it is. You can get the monster to bug out and sit right next to you allowing you to really get a close up. Its a nice comedy break in an otherwise serious story. I think that there was no need for monsters in this. The game could have just been about the rig failing no monsters and it would've been a 10/10 survival game against mother nature. The game also is purely a walking (crawling, jumping, and swimming) simulator. There isn't choice in anything and the paths are clearly marked with bright yellow things every ten feet. With the exception of a few water sections you can get turned around in, there isn't much here in terms of exploration which for how beautiful the game is is truly a shame. This, tied with very few (and mostly repeated) assets and things to interact with does make the game seem like a tech demo story more than a horror game. This isn't a bad thing once you accept this is a story, not a survival game. I actually didn't even remember adding this to my library, so I had no clue what I was in for. I had no expectations, and was blown away...just wishing that it was more of a survival horror game with how incredibly well executed most things here are.

Lastly, the voice acting in the game I thought was great. Paired with the graphics, its actually very believable that the characters you see are saying what they are. The atmosphere, the people, the emotions, it was done WELL. Kudos to the team, everyone on it.

Overall, I'd rate this an 8/10 and a worth it type of experience if you have a beefy computer and enjoy visual story games. If you are looking for something that will get your heart rate up, this isn't it. But, if you are looking for a highly atmospheric game that looks amazing and will have you invested in the characters and the conclusion, I can't recommend this more. Props to the development team.

name: Stellar Blade™
review:
TL;DR 89/100 Solid foundation held back by a few annoying things (no minimap/map in some areas, platforming is annoying and some puzzles as well as sidequests are insanely tedious) but a decent soulsborne with the potential to spawn a very successful sequel if they improve on mistakes that were made. Definitely worth at least giving it a try and picking up on sale. Don't treat it like a hack and slash. The combat rewards patience and precision and is very satisfying when you get the hang of it.

So I wanted to finish the two main endings to the game before writing a review and ended up putting a ton of hours in. First off Stellar Blade is a great game. Don't be deceived thinking it's some surface level fan service nonsense. If you want EVE to be running around with little to almost no clothing on and physics that make Newton roll around in his grave then go for it but there are plenty of outfits (exosuits) that are far less revealing and prone to "physics". 

To me Stellar Blade is sitting in an interesting position at about an 89/100. It's just shy of being an A and honestly if there were some slightly better map design choices, streamlined quests and general QoL I could see it pushing 95/100. The story isn't 10/10. It's interesting and despite complaints from others I don't find the characters to be "flat" or "lifeless". EVE, Adam, and Lily are all interesting to some degree and the VAs (in English as I played it) do a great job. I have had far worse experiences in games that people praise as "masterpieces" with characters that were far "flatter" and the audio quality sounded like it was recorded through a tin can. That said, I think there is a ton of potential for this story and that ShiftUp has done something interesting to set up what could be a very promising sequel. 

The combat appears to be hack and slash and the general provocative image people have of EVE invokes thoughts of titles like Bayonetta but this is not a hack and slash. It plays like a soulsborne. The combat revolves around a few simple combos and timed parries and dodges but it HEAVILY rewards patience and studying the movesets of your enemies. It has a "bonfire" mechanic with camps (some you can fast travel from, some you can't, and some are just purely fast travel points) and when you "rest" at a camp to replenish supplies (your estus flask equivalent is a "tumbler" potion with a few other consumables) all of the Naytibas (enemies) respawn save very major bosses/obstacles in typical soulsborne fashion. This is where the game can be both fun and tedious depending on what you are looking for and how much time you want to invest. There are several abilities that EVE gets later on as you progress through the game that make combat MUCH more reasonable (you do get a ranged weapon and yes there is a double jump but it is tied to a side quest later on so don't just keep jumping off dying somewhere because you can't "jump high enough" just come back after you get it which... there is a note on that later) so it really is in your best interest to focus on the core story at first to gain abilities and survivability instead of just struggling through the open areas as basic mobs tear you down as hard as the bosses can at first.

The open areas are a bit of a problem in that Stellar Blade can't exactly decide what it wants to be or what it wants to do in some situations and the side questing is one of the biggest problems there. There are two "open areas" that both unlock later on and they are both dreary deserts which is a bit of a bummer (it makes sense given the story and setting but you start to just see a lot of sand when running around collecting things and completing quests). Any platforming or parkour or laser jumping puzzles or bottom-less pits or........ really honestly anything that involves EVE having to jump around with accuracy and precision to get somewhere should have been cut entirely from the game or had an entire team dedicated to improving the platforming. Stellar Blade is at its best when it hits its soulsborne roots with satisfying combat and interesting combinations of gear and a plethora of enemies all with unique movesets to test your arsenal out on. The combat becomes pretty fluid and fun and even the boss mode from the main menu becomes enjoyable when you have the hang of it. 

My biggest complaints easily are the frustrating platforming, the complete and total lack of any map at all for several key areas (use something like map genie and save yourself the headache if you are getting collectibles) and just various QoL things like the absence of a minimap (you get a compass but the game really would benefit from a minimap) can be detrimental to the experience. 

With all of that said, I do find that the game excels in so many areas and some of the more frustrating/tedious aspects are optional content that you hardly have to even hit half of to get all three of the endings in two (if you time your saves right) playthroughs with a NG+. 

Something that a lot of people overlook or developers often just completely and totally forget are accessibility options and just general options for how the game UI appears/functions and various other settings and this is a game that EXCELS in that department. There are a ton of options to customize every control (even on a controller), turn the timer off on "puzzle boxes" (kinda like lockpicking minigames) and completely and totally simplify the fishing minigame making it a breeze. Also you can have QTEs auto succeed and on story difficulty the prompts for the more advanced inputs are displayed and help you adjust and it's worth playing around with if you are struggling with the combat. I can't praise ShiftUp enough for all of the accessibility features they have added. The game realizes something important in that it is a single player game so it doesn't matter if you want some extra time on puzzle boxes or find QTEs obnoxious. Having the ability to tinker with all of that is something every game should have. I understand the reasoning behind "the way the game was meant to be played" but there are a lot of people who aren't able to play the game the way the developers intended it to be played or the options/features are so lacking that the control schemes become so horrible that it can ruin a masterpiece. More devs and publishers need to follow ShiftUp's example here 100% Stellar Blade is fully a 10/10 in that department.

That the company who made a gachapon cover based waifu shooter for mobile went and created something at this level is honestly mind boggling. ShiftUp has something solid here to build a framework on and I am very excited for the sequel and hope that it improves on the areas where this game is lacking but doubles down on what really makes it enjoyable. 

Also if you are still in Eidos 7 (Silent Street/Haven't reached Xion yet) and having a bit of trouble with the beginning trust me try to at least push through to Xion and the game will open up and give you a lot more freedom in terms of what you do, how you do it, and your available equipment/combat options. I stand by my 89/100 rating in that I do feel the game is lacking just enough to push it into something grander or "goty" level but the foundation is there and it is totally worth grabbing.

Also side note on the DLCs, the NIER crossover is entirely cosmetic in rewards while the Nikke crossover introduces a minigame very akin to the mobile game (and it's quite frustrating if you're playing on a harder difficulty so put it onto story mode if it's bugging you) but it also introduces a number of cosmetics as well as a very interesting boss fight (in the boss rush mode after you have collected everything). I don't think the DLCs are really worth the full price for the content they have but they are worth picking up on sale for sure especially the Nikke one for the extra boss fight if you enjoy the game's combat.
note: worth a try if on sale, story isn't perfect, poor audio, combat can be tedious, boring, difficult platforming

Dnešní herní průmysl je plný her bez duše, bez srdce a bez odvahy. Už jsem pomalu ztrácel naději, ale Dawnwalker mě hned během prvních hodin přesvědčil o opaku. Z téhle hry je cítit obrovská vášeň a pečlivost a už to je poměrně vzácné.

review:
I purchased CoI sometime during the Update 3 phase. I could only get so far before things just fell apart, and I couldn't keep up with base infrastructure. name: Palworld
review:
Palworld has honestly been one of the most enjoyable survival games I've played. The combination of survival, base building, exploration, combat, and collecting Pals makes it really easy to lose hours in the game.

I'm playing co-op with a friend, and that's where the game really shines. Building bases together, exploring new areas, catching stronger Pals, fighting bosses, and slowly improving our setup has been a lot of fun.

There's a really satisfying sense of progression. At first you're just trying to survive and gather basic resources, and later you're managing multiple bases, breeding Pals, automating resources, crafting better equipment, and preparing for tougher areas.

The base-building and automation are probably my favorite parts. Watching your Pals actually work at your base and gradually turning a basic camp into a proper production setup feels great.

There are still some bugs and small performance issues, including occasional stutters and some Pal pathfinding problems, but none of them have stopped us from having a great time.

If you enjoy survival games, exploration, crafting, automation, and collecting creatures, Palworld is absolutely worth trying, especially if you have someone to play co-op with.

Absolutely recommending this game, great job Pocketpair!
note: some bugs, small performance issues

This game feels like digimon has finally hit a sweet spot were game complexity and creative story have reached a generally accessible level. Barrowing some of the simplicity that, that other franchise owned by nintendo were not talking about them, has developed over the years has made this digimon game easy to pick up and play while still having a decent level of complexity.

name: RuneScape: Dragonwilds
review:
I've played a ton of survival games. This is a game that does something that a lot of other survival type games don't do, and that's reward you for your time. The early game isn't a painful slog, you get new recipes and blueprints regularly, you get upgrades quickly. Nothing feels really over or under powered. Archery is good, magic is good melee is good. They do a great job of getting you engaged early and wanting to play more. It's not too hard, but it is challenging at times. 

The leveling system feels very dialed in, and you can feel your character progressing, hitting harder as you level your different offensive abilities. 

The magic system is a lot of fun and isn't just for attack, there's spells to help you farm, movement spells defensive spells and weapon enchants. 

There's a lot of nuance here, as you progress you get new little sub abilites connected to your differnt attacks. There's all kinds of audio "notifications" and alerts, if you listen for em that tell you things, like your arrow is ready to fire, or you just landed a critical hit. 

This is an adventure game with a side of survival crafting, which feels refreshing after years of punishing survival games with very little story and not much to do other than just survive. 

The build system is free of jank and actually makes sense. No jittering when trying to snap pieces in. There's lot of decorations early on. 

All in all this is a strong recommend. I'm still very early in, but had a hard time putting it down.

name: Borderlands 4
review:
++The one actually very good newly added thing is the manufacturer parts fitting on other weapon manufacturers. Gives a very fun weapon variety. Torgue guns with Jakobs accessory to make very high damage crits fly into another enemy nearby? Hell yeah!
Oh and perlescents are back now. That's actually neat. And a chance that your legendary can drop in a rainbow-colored skin is also neat.

+The vault hunters are good to play (some even very fun) and actually differ from one another.

+-The story is pretty meh. Don't really understand the high praise. Some story characters feel like some corporate slop. As if someone looked at data about generic things people in their 20s and 30s do/say (or just asked ChatGPT) and added that in. No real personality, just hollow shells. It also dosn't really help that they added the Vault Hunters from BL3 into the story. Everybody got alot older. But Moxxie is still alive looking like she just stepped from BL1 into this game (ridiculous, but tit-ehm Fan Bonus I assume...)

-The performance is utterly bad. Even with DLSS, you barely hit 60FPS. And trying to reduce graphic settings doesn't change anything. You can put everything on the lowest settings, making the game look worse than Borderlands 1 and having 60 FPS. But once you're in a fight, the FPS are dropping incredibly fast. Even below 20FPS in the end game.

-It just gets worse after every update.
The most recent update (10th Sep. 2026) just added a new DLC and another Character.
Which now means you can replay through the same 4 environments for the 6th time.
No new locations. Just the same layout recycled. What the actual fuck?!
Even Borderlands 1 had more variety to offer! But we got only 4 Vault Hunters for BL3.......

-A newly added feature (included in the update from 10th Sep. 2026) seems to be loaded textures without collision. You can now run through houses, vendors, walls, ammo crates, chests, stairs, etc. because only the texture layer has loaded in, but not the object with its collision. Meaning, you can also not interact with vendors, ammo crates, and such. Just wait 2 minutes till the area is fully loaded.
I just fell through the floor and stairs a couple of times. Oh, and enemies can just shoot through that texture, of course, because they apparently can see you trough it.

--DLCs are the biggest disappointment, though.
I really thought there would be amazing DLCs like in Borderlands 2 and 3. But it's just boring nonsense that feel like they could've been just another area in the main game, which you could get to via side quest(s). Reusing enemies, environments, and even bosses. Absolutely nothing new at all.

---Oh, and motherfucking cuntsucking bullshitting immunity phases and fixed damage points. See that enemy with the purple health bar? Yeah, just shoot at the 10 cm big hit points, which he has 5 of (if you don't have AOE), and when you've done that, either shoot these 5 - now floating around him- hit points to make them disappear or kill him fast enough before they reassemble, making him immune to damage and redoing this fucking shit again. And this utterly bullshit "gameplay feature" is throughout the entire game. Even bosses have this shit. Just so, that you dont oneshot anything, like you could in previous titles, because that would mean - less play time. Which is part of the reason why I have >260 hours. The other reason was collectibles, but you don't have to do that for every character anymore, just once with one character. (The first playthrough took me almost 90 hours, exploring the map and getting all the collectibles. Because the collectibles give you points, which can be used to increase the max. ammo. Second playthrough took me ~70hours) [it should be faster now though, because of guides, and sites like mapgenie].


TL;DR
If you're not huge into Borderlands, skip this one. Even if you just want to know what happened after the end of BL3. (This game doesn't really tell you anything new)
Utterly bad performance, barely any enemy and location variety, and annoying gameplay mechanics make this one (now, 1 year after the release and pretty much no performance updates or new DLCs [with a chance to add more variety to the game] in sight) now the worst Borderlands in the franchise.
Even worse than BL1, Wonderlands and Pre-Sequel. In that order.
And I paid 120€ for this trash. Definitely the first and last time I preordered a Borderlands game. And I had such high hopes after Borderlands 3... utterly dissappointed.
note: meh story, bad performance, worse after every update, poor combat, worse than previous games

name: CODE VEIN II
review:
This is "Code Vein" in name only. It is more of a reboot rather than a sequel. From what I gathered during the time I spent playing thus far, it has nothing to do with the original game and the new story they are telling is horribly confusing and convoluted, as well as painfully slow-paced as time padding, and thus completely unengaging (although that is subjective). Character creation is more limited than it was in the previous game, companions are about as one-dimensional in the first game, characters run like they made a doo-doo in their diapers, and combat feels like a downgrade from the previous installment, as it feels less... focused? If that makes sense. While I have not experienced any performance issues, there have been numerous odd visual glitches, especially during character creation, with animations either blurring together or fading out. Very odd.

All in all, this game is not engaging enough to retain my interest and I am not motivated enough to keep playing lest I exceed the playtime limit for a refund, and I do not want to be stuck with a disappointing game. They should have made this a story continuing the adventures of the previous characters and expanding on the world that game established.

Side note. Lou's thighs are so ridiculous with those itty-bitty shoulders it looks like a Skyrim mod. It is even more comical when I see her running in the corner of the screen with those awful stock-looking running animations. They would have been better off just copy-pasting the animations from the previous game.

[POST NOTE EDIT]
The more I thought about how the bad pacing of the story went, the more it reinforced my decision to refund the game. You watch a cutscene, go into character creation (which already disrupts the flow of the game), watch another cutscene, walk several feet and take a long ride up an elevator, watch another cutscene, interact with a character just to trigger another cutscene, get thrown into combat with three enemies that lasts for a single instant, and then have to watch yet another cutscene. And all the while you have to listen to the slow monotone expositions of the characters and watch your character slowly stare blankly, take a moment to think, and then silently nod to everything being told to them as they mindless go along with the plot because they are incapable of doing otherwise.

It is such unnecessary padding to stretch out your playtime that it completely disengaged me from the experience. I found myself constantly going "I don't care" as I was forced to watch another cutscene and listen to more confusing exposition.

I may pick this back up again in the future, as I want to fully be able to get into the open world aspect of the game, but not at the current asking price of admission (especially not the ultimate edition costing $100). I will get this during a Steam sale, or at the very least just purchase the base game with none of the additions, for it just isn't worth the extra cost.
note: worse than previous games, poor story, glitches, not worth value, boring
